A referendum offers a single model for Australia to become a republic: the Queen and Governor-General are replaced by a President chosen by a two-thirds majority of the Commonwealth Parliament. There is no prior popular vote among republic models. The Prime Minister publicly campaigns against the change. The President has weak independent legitimacy and can be removed through a process initiated by the Prime Minister.

A government-appointed task force drafts a single model in which the President is appointed by the Prime Minister with parliamentary confirmation. The model is put to referendum with no prior popular consultation; the Prime Minister actively campaigns for it.

A Cabinet-led process produces a model in which the President is selected by a joint sitting of the federal parliament on advice of the Prime Minister, by simple majority. No prior public deliberation is conducted; the referendum is a single yes/no on this model.

A Cabinet committee designs a model in which the President is appointed by the Prime Minister and confirmed by simple parliamentary majority. No prior public consultation on the design is conducted before the referendum.

A bipartisan parliamentary-leadership working group designs a model in which the President is appointed by the Prime Minister and Leader of the Opposition jointly. There is no public role in the design; the referendum is yes/no.

A Cabinet-drafted model proposes a President with both ceremonial and significant policy-coordination duties, appointed by the Prime Minister and removable by simple parliamentary majority. No prior public consultation is conducted.
A Cabinet-led model is put to referendum in which the President is chosen by the Prime Minister alone, subject to formal parliamentary acclamation. There is no prior public deliberation.
A Cabinet-drafted model proposes a President appointed by the Prime Minister for a five-year term, removable by a simple Cabinet motion. The model goes to referendum without any prior consultation.

A Cabinet-drafted model proposes a presidency vested in the Leader of the Government in the Senate, on Prime Ministerial nomination, with no prior public consultation; the referendum is offered as yes/no.

A government-commissioned constitutional-reform white paper produces a single model in which the President is selected by the Prime Minister with confirmation by a joint sitting of parliament. The model is sent to referendum with no prior consultation.
A Cabinet-drafted model proposes that the President be a former federal politician nominated by the Prime Minister and confirmed by simple parliamentary majority. There is no prior public input.

A Cabinet-led drafting committee designs a model in which the President is appointed by the Prime Minister with the requirement of consultation (not consent) from the Leader of the Opposition. No public input is sought; the referendum is yes/no.

A Cabinet-drafted model proposes a presidency selected by a board comprising the Prime Minister, Leader of the Opposition, and Cabinet Secretary, with no prior public deliberation and a final yes/no referendum.

A Cabinet committee produces a single model in which the President is chosen from a parliamentary shortlist by the Prime Minister, with removal triggered by Cabinet motion. There is no prior consultation.

A government Cabinet drafts a model in which the President is appointed by simple parliamentary majority on Prime Ministerial advice, with reserve powers that can be exercised on Cabinet direction. No prior public consultation is conducted.

A closed expert commission proposes a conservative republican model. The Crown is abolished, but the new President is selected by a council of former Governors-General, former Chief Justices, state Governors, and senior parliamentary figures. The public gets only a final yes/no referendum. The President is ceremonial, insulated from electoral politics, and removable only through a supermajority process.

A closed expert commission proposes a model in which the President is selected by a council of state Governors and the Chief Justice, serves a single non-renewable seven-year ceremonial term, and can be removed only by a parliamentary supermajority on a judicial finding of incapacity. The public gets only a yes/no referendum.

A government-appointed constitutional commission designs a model in which the President is nominated by a panel of retired judges and confirmed by a two-thirds joint sitting of parliament. The role is ceremonial; removal requires a supermajority on incapacity grounds. There is no prior public input.

A constitutional council of former Chief Justices designs a model in which the President is selected by their council and confirmed by a parliamentary supermajority. The role is purely ceremonial. Only a final yes/no referendum is offered.

A government white paper proposes a model in which the President is nominated by a Council of State comprising former state Premiers and Chief Justices, with a two-thirds joint sitting confirmation. The duties are ceremonial only; removal requires both judicial and parliamentary findings. There is no prior public deliberation.

A bipartisan parliamentary commission designs a model in which the President is appointed by an Eminent Persons Council and serves a single seven-year ceremonial term, removable only by a two-thirds joint sitting on a judicial-misconduct finding. There is no public role in the design.

A constitutional drafting committee proposes that the President be selected by a council of former Governors-General and confirmed by parliamentary supermajority. The role is ceremonial only; removal requires a constitutional-court ruling and a parliamentary supermajority. There is no public input.

A government-appointed expert commission designs a model in which the President is selected by an elite panel of senior public-service heads and confirmed by a two-thirds Senate vote. The role is ceremonial; removal requires a judicial finding plus a parliamentary supermajority. No prior public consultation is conducted.

A constitutional-design conference of senior judges and academic constitutional lawyers produces a model in which the President is selected by their conference and confirmed by parliamentary supermajority. The role is ceremonial only. The public role is limited to a final yes/no.

A closed government drafting team designs a model in which the President is appointed by a Council of State (comprising former state Governors and Chief Justices), serves a single ceremonial term, and is removable only by judicial determination plus a parliamentary supermajority. There is no prior public deliberation.

A federal-and-states constitutional commission designs a model in which the President is nominated by a joint state-and-territory upper-house council and confirmed by parliamentary supermajority. The role is ceremonial only; removal is by supermajority. There is no prior public input.

A closed constitutional-experts panel proposes that the President be nominated by an Eminent Australians Council and confirmed by a two-thirds joint sitting. The role is ceremonial; supermajority removal applies on an incapacity finding. There is no prior public deliberation.

A constitutional-design working group of former Governors-General and Chief Justices proposes that the President be selected by their council and confirmed by parliamentary supermajority, with codified reserve powers. There is no public input.

A government commission of former High Court justices designs a model in which the President is selected by their commission and confirmed by a parliamentary supermajority. The role is purely ceremonial. The public votes only on the model.

A closed expert constitutional-design panel proposes a model in which the President is selected by a Council of State comprising former Prime Ministers, Chief Justices, and state Governors, with a parliamentary supermajority confirmation. The role is ceremonial only; removal requires supermajority. There is no prior public deliberation.

A citizens' deliberation process recommends a direct-election republic. Australians would elect a ceremonial President by national vote. The reserve powers are codified, the President cannot sit in Parliament, and dismissal requires a transparent constitutional process. The model is put to a final referendum after extensive public deliberation.

A national citizens' assembly process recommends a model in which the President is directly elected by Australians by national popular vote every five years. The reserve powers are codified, the President is barred from political-party affiliation, and removal requires a transparent constitutional-court process. A final referendum follows extensive public deliberation.

A multi-state deliberative-democracy process recommends a model in which the President is directly elected by Australians using a preferential national vote. The role is ceremonial with codified reserve powers. A national referendum follows extensive public deliberation.

A citizens' jury and national town-hall process produces a model in which the President is directly elected by national popular vote on a non-party-affiliated ballot, with codified ceremonial duties and transparent dismissal procedures. A national referendum follows the deliberation.

A national citizens' assembly process recommends a direct-election model with codified reserve powers, restrictions on prior political-party leadership in the previous decade, and a judicially supervised removal process. A national referendum follows extensive deliberation.

A multi-stage public-consultation process produces a model in which the President is directly elected by national popular vote with a six-year non-renewable term, codified ceremonial powers, and party-affiliation restrictions. A national referendum follows extensive consultation.

A national citizens' assembly recommends a model in which the President is directly elected by all Australians using ranked-choice voting. The role is ceremonial with codified reserve powers; political-party affiliation is prohibited. A referendum follows substantial deliberation.

A multi-year deliberative-democracy process recommends a direct-election model with a five-year non-renewable term, codified powers, judicially supervised removal, and restrictions on prior political careers. A national referendum follows.

A citizens' assembly process produces a direct-election model with codified ceremonial powers and supermajority parliamentary removal supplementing a judicial-misconduct finding. A final referendum follows substantial public deliberation.

A national series of constitutional conventions and citizens' assemblies recommends a model in which the President is directly elected by national popular vote on a non-political-party ballot. The role is ceremonial with codified reserve powers. A referendum follows.

A multi-state citizens' assembly process produces a model in which the President is directly elected by Australians using a preferential national vote, with codified ceremonial powers and a strict ban on prior political-party leadership. A national referendum follows.

A national civic-deliberation process recommends a direct-election model with a single seven-year term, codified ceremonial duties, and constitutional-court-supervised removal. A referendum follows extensive consultation.

A national deliberative process produces a model in which the President is directly elected by national popular vote every four years, with codified powers, party-affiliation restrictions, and a transparent removal mechanism. A referendum follows.

A national citizens' assembly process recommends a model in which the President is directly elected by ranked-choice national vote with codified ceremonial duties and judicially supervised removal. A final referendum follows substantial public consultation.

A multi-year national deliberative-democracy process produces a direct-election model with codified powers, restrictions on past parliamentary careers, and a constitutional-court-led removal procedure. A national referendum follows.

A randomly selected citizens' assembly, state representatives, and civic organisations nominate a shortlist of non-partisan candidates. The public then chooses one in a national confirmation vote. The President is ceremonial, the reserve powers are codified, and removal requires both judicial certification of incapacity or misconduct and a parliamentary supermajority. The whole model is put to a final constitutional referendum.

A citizens' assembly process produces a model in which a randomly selected citizens' assembly nominates a shortlist of non-partisan candidates, the public chooses one in a national vote, and the model is ratified by a final referendum. The President is ceremonial, with codified reserve powers and dual judicial-and-parliamentary removal.

A multi-state deliberative process produces a model in which a Council of Eminent Australians nominates a shortlist confirmed by a public ratification vote. The President serves a single seven-year ceremonial term, with codified powers and judicial-plus-parliamentary supermajority removal. A final referendum follows extensive deliberation.

A national citizens' assembly process recommends a model in which a bipartisan parliamentary committee combined with a civil-society panel nominates candidates, the public votes on the shortlist, and the model is ratified by a final referendum. The President is ceremonial with codified powers and supermajority removal.

A long-form deliberative process produces a model in which a citizens' jury nominates two finalists, the public chooses one, and the model is adopted by referendum. The role is purely ceremonial with codified reserve powers and a judicial-plus-supermajority removal mechanism.

A multi-year deliberative-democracy process produces a model in which a citizens' assembly nominates non-partisan candidates with parliamentary cross-bench endorsement, the public ratifies one by national vote, and a final referendum adopts the model. The President is ceremonial with codified powers and judicially supervised removal.

A national citizens' assembly process produces a model in which a panel of citizens, ex-judges, and civic leaders jointly nominates a shortlist, the public chooses among them, and the model is adopted by referendum. The role is ceremonial with codified powers and supermajority removal.

A multi-state deliberative process produces a model in which a citizens' assembly and a parliamentary cross-bench committee jointly nominate candidates, the public ratifies one, and the model is adopted by referendum. The role is ceremonial, with codified powers and dual-track removal.

A long-form citizens' assembly process produces a model in which a randomly selected nominations panel proposes non-partisan candidates, the public votes among them, and the model is adopted by a final referendum. The role is ceremonial, with codified powers, and supermajority removal supplemented by judicial determination.

A national civic deliberation produces a model in which a citizens' jury and a panel of retired judges jointly nominate three candidates, the public chooses one, and the model is ratified by referendum. The role is ceremonial with codified powers and dual judicial-parliamentary removal.

A multi-year deliberative process produces a model in which a citizens' assembly nominates candidates from a vetted civil-society pool, the public ratifies the chosen candidate, and the model is adopted by referendum. The role is ceremonial with codified powers and supermajority removal.

A national citizens' assembly process recommends a model in which a bipartisan and citizens' nominations committee proposes non-partisan candidates, the public chooses, and the model is adopted by referendum. The role is ceremonial with codified powers and judicially supervised supermajority removal.

A national deliberative-democracy process produces a model in which a citizens' jury and a council of former state Governors jointly nominate candidates, the public chooses, and the model is adopted by referendum. The role is ceremonial with codified powers and supermajority removal.

A long-form public-deliberation process produces a model in which a citizens' assembly and a panel of civil-society leaders jointly nominate non-partisan candidates, the public ratifies the choice, and the model is adopted by referendum. The role is ceremonial with codified powers and dual-track removal.

A multi-year national constitutional convention process produces a model in which a citizens' assembly nominates non-partisan candidates with judicial-vetting endorsement, the public chooses, and the model is adopted by referendum. The role is ceremonial with codified powers and supermajority removal.
